name: Chicago Zen Center
technique: Shikantaza and koan-introspection zazen, formal sesshin practice with teisho and dokusan
teacherAccess: Daily teisho and dokusan with the Sensei/Abbot and Head of Zendo during sesshin; ongoing teacher access for formal students
retreatOptions: 4-6 day live-in sesshins, held about 5 times a year, accommodating up to 24 people; part- or short-time attendance possible by arrangement
schedule: Sesshin days run roughly 4:30am to 9:25pm bedtime, structured into four blocks with formal zazen rounds, chanting services, a daily work period, calisthenics, three rest periods, and daily teisho with dokusan offered three times a day
cost: Sesshin involves a fee to cover food and lodging (exact published amount not listed on site); financial assistance available via the Abbot's Fund for those unable to afford it; ongoing practice at the Center itself is offered free of charge
workNotes: All sesshin participants are assigned a job (kitchen or housekeeping) for the duration and take part in a daily work period; outside of sesshin, members may join sangha work days and general upkeep volunteering.
foodNotes: Breakfast and dinner during sesshin are formal, chanted meals prepared onsite as part of the retreat; specific ingredients/diet type not detailed on site but consistent with typical Zen center vegetarian fare.
about: Chicago Zen Center is a Zen Buddhist temple in Evanston, Illinois, in the Rochester (Kapleau) lineage founded by Philip Kapleau Roshi. The center's building accommodates up to 24 people for live-in, multi-day sesshin retreats held about five times a year, ranging from four to six days, including formal zazen, chanting, daily work periods, and dokusan with the resident teacher. Outside of sesshin, the center offers a full schedule of regular sittings, introductory practice sessions, and paths toward formal study, precepts, and ordination, and it welcomes practitioners from other Dharma traditions to its retreats. Day-to-day practice at the center is offered free of charge, with only sesshin carrying a fee to cover food and lodging, and financial assistance is available for those who cannot afford it. Longer-term residential training (minimum one-year commitment) is also available to members for a monthly fee.
